source.title: PaLI: A Jointly-Scaled Multilingual Language-Image Model
source.authors: Xi Chen; Xiao Wang; Soravit Changpinyo; A. Piergiovanni; Piotr Padlewski; Daniel M. Salz; Sebastian Goodman; Adam Grycner; Basil Mustafa; Lucas Beyer; Alexander Kolesnikov; J. Puigcerver; Nan Ding; Ke-Ran Rong; Hassan Akbari; Gaurav Mishra; Lin-Ting Xue; Ashish V. Thapliyal; James Bradbury; Wei-Cheng Kuo; Mojtaba Seyedhosseini; Chao Jia; Burcu Karagol Ayan; C. Riquelme; A. Steiner; A. Angelova; Xiao-Hua Zhai; N. Houlsby; Radu Soricut

record.tranche_reason: The paper reports how downstream scores change with model scale in a multilingual vision-language setting, but does not test language-model held-out cross-entropy scaling laws.
record.gate_note: The paper cites language-model scaling work, but its own scaling experiments report downstream benchmark scores for PaLI variants—not held-out pretraining cross-entropy, fitted power laws, extrapolation from small runs, or compute-optimal parameter/token allocations. Rows below bear on downstream performance with scale (V6).
record.test_reason: The paper reports its own downstream scores for PaLI vision-language models at 0.7B–17B parameters, so it bears on V6's 'downstream improves with scale' in a multimodal setting. It fits no curve and reports no pretraining loss, so predictability itself is not tested. Size changes are confounded with which component is scaled (mT5 vs ViT), learning rate and, for some tables, resolution or the high-res phase.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors conclude that jointly scaling the vision and language components improves vision-language performance with no saturation at 17B, and that scaling the vision side gives a better return per parameter.
record.recipe_differences: This is a multimodal model-scaling study measuring downstream benchmark performance, not a reproduction of the original language-model loss-scaling measurements or compute-optimal allocation analysis.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported scaling comparisons vary component sizes and, in some experiments, image resolution or training setup. The paper notes that PaLI-5B used a slightly different training mixture and hyperparameters; the high-resolution pretraining phase also adds performance.

fits_no_version.finding: Scaling the ViT backbone from ViT-G to ViT-e gives only marginal gains on vision-only ImageNet few-shot (84.9→85.2) but larger gains on vision-language tasks.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Returns to scaling a vision encoder saturate on image classification but not on vision-language tasks.

record.problems: The scaling evidence is from a limited set of selected multimodal model sizes and downstream benchmarks, not fitted scaling curves or held-out pretraining loss. The paper notes that PaLI-5B used a slightly different mixture and hyperparameters; no uncertainty estimates are given for the reported scores.
record.rows_left_out: No relevant rows left out. The paper reports many other downstream benchmark results, but they are not included unless they are part of the selected scale comparisons recorded here.

untested.parts: Whether gains are predictable (no fitted trend or extrapolation), and any link between pretraining loss and downstream score.
No power-law fit for vision-language loss or performance; only 3–4 model sizes.

missing.what: PaLI-3B/15B/17B scores on VQAv2, TextVQA, VizWiz-QA, ST-VQA, NoCaps, TextCaps and VizWiz-Cap. PaLI-17B results include the high-res phase, which confounds them.
missing.locator: Tables 1 and 3; Figure 2 (seven-task average, +3.1 language, +3.2 vision)

missing.what: Crossmodal-3600 multilingual CIDEr, PaLI-3B vs PaLI-17B (35-language average 47.0→53.6)
Top-5 zero-shot ImageNet-family accuracy across sizes
ViT-g/G/e scaling on ImageNet few-shot, COCO and VQAv2

record.verdict_notes: This is a multimodal model, not a text language model, so V6 applies only loosely. There are only 3–4 sizes, and size is confounded with component choice, learning rate and resolution. No uncertainty is reported. The record's 'reversed' state for r11 overstates a 0.08-point dip.

versions.untested_parts: No power-law fit to held-out pretraining loss over parameters, tokens, or compute.
No extrapolation from small runs to much larger runs.
No fixed-compute allocation sweep or fitted parameter/token scaling with compute.
No comparison of depth, width, or architecture at fixed parameter count.
The paper studies a vision-language model, but does not test whether a power-law form holds for loss in other modalities or training regimes.
Tests changes in downstream benchmark scores across selected model sizes; does not fit a predictive relationship, report held-out pretraining loss, or test whether loss predicts downstream scores.
No analysis of fitted exponents, setup-dependent law disagreements, or bending of power-law curves.

relationships.condition: PaLI 3B→17B and 700M→17B on zero-shot ImageNet-family classification, COCO-Cap, OKVQA and TallyQA
relationships.reason: Scores rise with size in nearly all comparisons, e.g. OKVQA 52.4→62.4 and TallyQA 62.4→71.9 (r3, r6, r8, r9, r12, r15, r18, r22, r24–r26, r28, r29, r31, r32, r34, r35).
relationships.display_finding: Scores increased with size in nearly all comparisons, including OKVQA from 52.4 to 62.4 and TallyQA from 62.4 to 71.9.

relationships.condition: Scaling only the language component (PaLI-3B→15B, ~5x parameters) on zero-shot ImageNet variants and COCO
relationships.reason: Gains are negligible or slightly negative: ImageNet +0.21, INet-v2 +0.26, Sketch −0.08, COCO +0.8 (r2, r11, r14, r17, r21). Gains depend on which component is scaled, not on total parameters.
relationships.display_finding: Increasing PaLI from 3B to 15B changed ImageNet by +0.21, INet-v2 by +0.26, Sketch by −0.08, and COCO by +0.8.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Most reported PaLI size comparisons on ImageNet-family zero-shot classification, COCO-Cap, OKVQA, and TallyQA
reader_labels.reason: Scores rise with scale in these tested comparisons; see r2–r9, r12, r14–r18, r20–r26, r28–r29, r31–r32, and r34–r35. The paper also describes improvements across its seven V&L scaling benchmarks.
